anchors.subject: a transfer query (Z3Py)
anchors.claim: unsat, therefore safe.
anchors.requirement: Every transfer the service accepts leaves the sender at zero or above, and the service does accept transfers: a positive amount, up to the sender's balance, within any configured cap.
anchors.scenarioQuestion: Does the statement speak about this transfer: do these values meet every premise it checks?

basedOn.incident: PutnamBench issue #361: a readability refactor lost parentheses, an implication absorbed a chain of conjunctions, and the hypotheses became inconsistent; automated hypothesis-redundancy checks found it.

cases.claim: unsat, therefore safe.
cases.description: Adds the per-transfer cap from config.toml to the query. Z3 still answers unsat: no accepted transfer overdraws the sender.
statement: a, b, amount = Ints('a b amount')
s.add(a - amount < 0)   # the violation: the sender ends below zero
diff: a, b, amount = Ints('a b amount')

scenarios.text: a = 10, b = 0, amount = 3
scenarios.why: Every premise holds, so the unsat speaks about this transfer: the sender ends at 7.
scenarios.keyLine: [q1 s1 a=10 b=0 amount=3] sat (covered)

scenarios.text: a = 10, b = 0, amount = 150
scenarios.why: 150 is over the cap of 100, so the query never considers it.
scenarios.keyLine: [q1 s2 a=10 b=0 amount=150] unsat (not covered)

scenarios.text: a = 2, b = 0, amount = 5
scenarios.why: The guard amount <= a excludes it: an overdraft the service refuses is outside the statement.

scenarios.why: Exactly at the cap, and within the balance: covered.

cases.claim: unsat, therefore safe.
cases.description: Inlines refund_allowed()'s window check into the refund query. Still unsat.
statement: paid, refund, days = Ints('paid refund days')
s.add(days >= 0, days <= 30)    # the refund window, in days since payment
s.add(days < 31)                # the window check, inlined from refund_allowed()

diff: s.add(days >= 0, days <= 30)    # the refund window, in days since payment
+s.add(days < 31)                # the window check, inlined from refund_allowed()
s.add(paid - refund < 0)        # the violation: more refunded than was paid

anchors.subject: a two-party transfer query (Z3Py)
anchors.claim: No balance can go negative; the transfer is safe.
anchors.requirement: ledger.go keeps every balance as a Go int64, whose arithmetic wraps on overflow. Every transfer it accepts, computed as ledger.go computes it, leaves the sender and the recipient at zero or above.
anchors.scenarioQuestion: Does the statement speak about this transfer: do these values meet every premise it checks?

basedOn.incident: Bitcoin CVE-2010-5139: a transaction's outputs overflowed when summed, so the client's check that outputs do not exceed inputs passed, and the block created about 184 billion bitcoins.
basedOn.dateMarks: the block with the overflowing transaction was mined

cases.claim: No balance can go negative; the transfer is safe.
cases.description: Extends the overdraft check to the recipient. Z3 answers unsat: no balance can go negative.
statement: a, b, amount = Ints('a b amount')
s.add(amount > 0, amount <= a)              # ledger.go: the transfer guard
s.add(amount <= 2**63 - 1 - b)              # ledger.go: the recipient's overflow check
s.add(Or(a - amount < 0, b + amount < 0))   # the violation: a balance ends below zero
diff: s.add(amount <= 2**63 - 1 - b)              # ledger.go: the recipient's overflow check
-s.add(a - amount < 0)                       # the violation: the sender ends below zero
+s.add(Or(a - amount < 0, b + amount < 0))   # the violation: a balance ends below zero

scenarios.text: a = 10, b = 0, amount = 3
scenarios.why: Every premise holds, so the unsat speaks about this transfer. In int64 the run gives the sender 7 and the recipient 3, the same as over Int.
scenarios.keyLine: [q1 s1 a=10 b=0 amount=3] sat (covered)

scenarios.why: The overflow check refuses it: b + amount would pass the largest int64. ledger.go refuses it too, so the statement leaves it out for the right reason.
scenarios.keyLine: [q1 s2 a=10 b=9223372036854775800 amount=10] unsat (not covered)

scenarios.text: a = 2, b = 0, amount = 5
scenarios.why: The guard amount <= a refuses an overdraft, so the query never considers it.
scenarios.keyLine: [q1 s3 a=2 b=0 amount=5] unsat (not covered)

scenarios.why: The recipient lands exactly on the largest int64, 9223372036854775807 in the run's int64 line: in range, and covered.
scenarios.keyLine: [q1 s4 a=5 b=9223372036854775802 amount=5] sat (covered)

cases.explain: The overflow check keeps b + amount inside int64, and the guard keeps a - amount at zero or above, so every operation the query models stays in range and Int arithmetic agrees with ledger.go's. The same premises over 64-bit bit-vectors are unsat too: the claim holds for both parties as ledger.go computes them.

keyLines: [1.5 BitVec64 signed: guarded DESTINATION wrap] sat
cases.explain: The query is over unbounded Int, and the code is int64. Nothing in the premises keeps b + amount below 2^63, so the unsat says nothing about what ledger.go computes: over 64-bit bit-vectors the same premises admit a recipient that wraps negative. The guard protects the sender, not the recipient.

scenarios.why: The guard refuses it.
scenarios.keyLine: [q3 s4 a=2 amount=5] unsat (not covered)

cases.explain: Over Int a negative amount only raises the sender, so the unsat looks harmless. ledger.go's amount is an int64: near its minimum, a - amount wraps, and over 64-bit bit-vectors the same premises admit a sender that ends negative (RUN-z3-bv64-negamt records the same wrap).

cases.claim: unsat: no transfer can overdraw the sender.
cases.description: Drops amount > 0 from the query: the guard already bounds the amount. Z3 still answers unsat.
statement: # ledger.go: func transfer(a, b int64, amount uint32) (int64, int64)
s.add(amount >= 0)                  # ledger.go: amount is a uint32
s.add(amount <= a)                  # ledger.go: the transfer guard
s.add(a - amount < 0)               # the violation: the sender ends below zero
diff: s.add(amount >= 0)                  # ledger.go: amount is a uint32
s.add(amount <= a)                  # ledger.go: the transfer guard

scenarios.why: amount >= 0 leaves it out, and a uint32 cannot hold -5, so ledger.go never receives it.

cases.explain: amount is a uint32 widened to int64, so it is never negative and a - amount stays between 0 and a: every operation is in range, and the query keeps amount >= 0 from the type. Dropping amount > 0 only admits a zero transfer. Over 64-bit bit-vectors, with amount widened from 32 bits, the violation is unsat too.

anchors.subject: a refund theorem (Lean)
anchors.claim: Refunds never overdraw anyone; proved.
anchors.requirement: If every balance is at zero or above before a refund of a non-negative amount, every balance is at zero or above after it: the customer's, the merchant's and every other account's.
anchors.scenarioQuestion: Does the theorem, as written, rule out this outcome?

basedOn.incident: Spec-Harness: on SpecGenBench, 22.7% of the specifications a verifier accepted had no postcondition, so the verifier's acceptance said nothing about what the code must do.
basedOn.dateMarks: the paper's first arXiv version was posted

cases.claim: Refunds never overdraw anyone; proved.
cases.description: Replaces the sorry in refund_nonneg with a proof. The build is green.
statement: def NonNeg (s : State) : Prop := ∀ j, 0 ≤ s.balance j
def refund (s : State) (p : PaymentId) (amt : Int) : State :=
if j = (s.payments p).merchant then s.balance j - amt
else if j = (s.payments p).customer then s.balance j + amt

scenarios.text: Customer 0, merchant 30. A refund of 50 leaves the customer at 50 and the merchant at -20.
scenarios.why: Every balance was at zero or above and 50 is non-negative, so NonNeg must hold afterwards; a merchant at -20 breaks it. (The refund itself refuses this one: the run shows the balances unchanged at 0 and 30.)

cases.explain: The build, the axioms and the kernel replay are all clean, and the theorem is true. But its conclusion names only the payment's customer: an outcome that leaves the merchant at -20 meets the theorem, so it proves less than 'never overdraw anyone'. This refund does refuse that outcome; the proof does not show it, and an unguarded refund satisfies the same statement while the merchant goes negative (RUN-lean-refund-a21: refund_nonneg and refund_breaks_inv both check).

anchors.subject: an obligation checked without a guard (SMT-LIB)
anchors.claim: Z3 proved the invariant obligation, even without the guard.
anchors.requirement: The query Z3 checked implies the command's whole invariant obligation: from any state that meets Inv, as the ledger declares it, every step the command takes ends in a state that meets every conjunct of Inv.

statement: # Init: bal >= 0 and held == 0. The invariant to keep: bal >= 0.
def step(s, t, n):                               # the agent's commands: one step from s to t
And(n <= bal, held2 == held + n, bal2 == bal),           # Hold(n)
And(n <= held, held2 == held - n, bal2 == bal - n),      # Capture(n)
And(n <= held, held2 == held - n, bal2 == bal)))         # Release(n)

anchors.subject: a search view's noninterference check (Z3Py)
anchors.claim: Noninterference proved for the document view.
anchors.requirement: A client of an Acme user cannot tell apart two worlds that differ only in another tenant's private documents, by anything the response carries: its JSON body, its result count, its status code.
anchors.scenarioQuestion: Does the statement's observer tell these two responses apart?

basedOn.incident: The PostgreSQL 18 row-security documentation warns that integrity checks such as unique constraints bypass row security, so an error can tell a user about rows they cannot see: a covert channel.

cases.claim: Noninterference proved for the document view.
cases.description: Adds a result count to the search response, then re-runs the noninterference check. Z3 answers unsat.
statement: hits  = count([And(e, r, m) for e, r, m in W])   # readable matches: the JSON body
total = count([And(e, r, m) for e, r, m in W])   # the result count
def observe(hits, total):                            # what the proof compares
L, R = world('L'), world('R')                        # three document slots each
s.add(rel(L, R))                                     # Rel: the worlds agree on what Acme may know
s.add(Or([a != b for a, b in zip(observe(*search(L)), observe(*search(R)))]))

anchors.subject: a tenant-isolation check for a sharing release (Z3Py)
anchors.claim: No tenant can ever observe any change in another tenant.
anchors.requirement: Acme sees nothing of Birch's beyond what the product releases on purpose: the title and body of each document Birch shares with Acme, as Birch edits them, for as long as the share lasts; and the platform-wide document count on every tenant's usage panel. Everything else of Birch's stays out of Acme's view.
anchors.scenarioQuestion: Does the statement allow this behavior?

anchors.subject: a validated SQL rewrite (PostgreSQL)
anchors.claim: Generated SQL validated; equivalent to the source.
anchors.requirement: On every database the schema allows, the generated SQL gives the outcome of what it replaces: it commits or aborts alike, and leaves the same table. A validation report says how far its method reaches: every database, a stated bound, or a number of instances tried.
anchors.scenarioQuestion: On this database, do the generated SQL and what it is checked against give the same outcome: the same commit or abort and the same table after, or for a query the same result?

basedOn.incident: Singh and Bedathur report that LLM judges of SQL query equivalence lean towards answering 'equivalent'; a CIDR 2026 study of LLM SQL rewrites found that about 32% of them changed query results.
basedOn.dateMarks: the first arXiv version of the judges paper

cases.claim: Generated SQL validated; equivalent to the source.
cases.description: Rewrites the compiled credit as an upsert, which the new storage layer prefers. The validator accepts it.
statement: -- schema: acct (id int PRIMARY KEY, bal bigint NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0))
-- the compiled credit of transfer 30 1 2; the plan aborts unless it touches one row
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 30 WHERE id = 2;
INSERT INTO acct (id, bal) SELECT id, bal + 30 FROM acct WHERE id = 2
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET bal = EXCLUDED.bal;
method  replay both on every database with ids in {1, 2}, each absent, at 0 or at 50: 9 databases
diff: -UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + $amt WHERE id = $to;
+INSERT INTO acct (id, bal) SELECT id, bal + $amt FROM acct WHERE id = $to
+  ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET bal = EXCLUDED.bal;
